item.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

China’s Huawei found guilty of trade secrets conspiracy, fraud in US trial

But jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced of engaging in criminal racketeering conspiracy.

A United States jury has convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.

However, jurors on Tuesday acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge is typically used in organised crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from US companies.

The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere.

Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.

US authorities had targeted Huawei for years, saying the company posed national security risks.

The criminal case began in 2018, and the following year the US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology.

Experts have said the case has not undermined Huawei’s business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China’s push for artificial intelligence.

The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.

Huawei and three affiliates faced 12 charges, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets and obstruct justice.

Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that did not actually exist.

Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but saw the racketeering conspiracy acquittal as vindication.

“That was the only count that brought all of the allegations together,” and the jury rejected it, he said outside court, saying that the verdict “repudiated the central government narrative in the case”.

It is unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to US carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and the United Kingdom.

Founder’s daughter detained

The case emerged in December 2018 when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s chief financial officer and daughter of the company’s founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the US, China and Canada.

Meng had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.

She fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero’s welcome. The charges against her were dropped.

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran.

Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades.

During the trial, prosecutors tried to prove Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel’s antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX.

Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device.

Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng’s deferred prosecution agreement, in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

Banks knew

The defence argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei’s business in Iran and were competing for Huawei’s business.

Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having “cherry-picked” a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy.

He said Huawei succeeded through “hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development”.

Huawei has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

item.title: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter.

Dell shares rose in extended trading.

Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:

- EPS: $9.45, adjusted, versus $6.59 expected

- Revenue: $54.94 billion, versus $49.32 billion expected

Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.

The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.

The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.

ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.

"We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.

In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery.

"That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell.

The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through.

"Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts.

The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion.

The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer.

Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends.

Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

item.title: Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Colombian president blames ex-FARC rebels for car bomb blast

Colombian President says Villavicencio bomb attack came in retaliation of government offensives.

Car bomb strikes governor’s office in Meta, Colombia

Bogota, Colombia – Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has blamed ex-FARC rebels for a car bomb attack last night targeting a state government building, which injured at least 23 people.

On a visit to Villavicencio on Tuesday, where the attack took place, the president accused Antonio Medina, a commander of the Central General Staff (EMC) rebel group, of plotting the bombing in retaliation for government offensives in the province.

“The bandit Antonio Medina from the [FARC] dissidents is to blame, and we’re going to go after him and make him pay with blood,” de la Espriella told reporters.

Last night’s attack rocked the seat of government in Meta, a province bordering the capital, Bogota, to the southeast. Videos show extensive damage to the building in Villavicencio, which houses the governor’s office, as well as surrounding businesses and vehicles.

The Head of National Police Operations, Ricardo Alarcon, told local media that initial tests indicate the car was laden with between 80 and 100kg (176-220 pounds) of pentolite, a high explosive used in military warheads, as well as civilian mining.

Meta was a historical heartland for the FARC, which officially demobilised following a historic peace deal in 2016. In the years since, dissident rebels who refused to lay down their arms or returned to war have expanded their control in the province, a key access point to the coca plantations, gold mining and drug smuggling routes of the Amazon River Basin.

The most powerful group is the EMC, headed by alias Ivan Mordisco, one of Colombia’s most wanted men. The government earlier this year announced a bounty of 5 billion pesos (roughly $1.4m) for his capture or killing.

In recent months, the government has increased pressure on the EMC, bombing its camps and targeting senior members. Just yesterday, the president confirmed the killing of alias El Churco, an EMC commander.

The campaign is part of the new far-right government’s security pivot, which aims to tackle criminal organisations through military force and has suspended the negotiations initiated under the previous government.

De la Espriella has suggested that last night’s bombing in Villavicencio was likely a retaliation against ramped-up state pressure on armed groups.

“The narco-terrorists are running wild, launching desperate attacks, because they know we are defeating them and that their end is near,” the president wrote on X this morning.

The attack, which happened on the eve of the 10-year anniversary of the 2016 peace deal, highlights the growing risks to civilians under de la Espriella’s heavy-handed security strategy, say experts.

“As the government increases pressure, armed and criminal groups are trying to raise the cost of doing that for the government by exerting pain, instilling fear and causing direct harm against communities and against the civilian population,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-24 21:45 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering

Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

Following the verdict, Huawei said the five trade secret-related charges "were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades".

"No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation," the company said.

"We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests."

item.title: Saudi national charged in OpenAI bugging to be released on $1 million bond
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk.

"We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.

Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."

Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.

Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including

dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."

Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.

Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.

— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

This is developing news. Check back for updates.

Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback sends AI videos into overdrive

Issued on:

Just 11 days after resigning as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang’s return has unleashed a fresh wave of AI-generated videos. But the internet has changed its tune: while last week’s memes mocked Huang, many now celebrate his comeback. One viral video purportedly showing him dancing is actually AI-manipulated footage of a basketball coach from 2016. From humiliation to hero worship, the technology Nvidia helped popularise is rewriting the narrative surrounding its own CEO, as Vedika Bahl explains.

Just 11 days after stepping down as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang returned to the helm of the world's leading AI chipmaker on Monday, unleashing a fresh wave of AI-generated videos. But the internet appears to have changed its tune: while last week's memes mocked Huang following his resignation, many are now celebrating his comeback.

Nvidia's board announced on Monday that it had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as CEO, following his resignation amid a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs and espionage allegations. The reversal came despite the board previously saying it had no plans to reinstate him, and after US President Donald Trump said he had personally intervened.

Huang received a warm welcome from employees upon his return to Nvidia's headquarters, with genuine footage showing him being greeted with applause and hugs. But within hours of the announcement, AI-generated videos purporting to show his celebrations began circulating on social media.

Viral dancing video is AI-manipulated

One video, which has racked up millions of views across TikTok, X and Instagram, appears to show Huang dancing his way into a room before being surrounded by a cheering crowd. Many users shared the footage alongside captions declaring that "the king is back".

However, the video has nothing to do with Nvidia. The original footage is a well known internet clip, and was published on YouTube in March 2016 by the University of North Carolina's basketball team, the Tar Heels. It shows players celebrating in a locker room after defeating their rivals, Duke University.

The man dancing at the centre of the celebrations is the team's then-head coach, Roy Williams. A side-by-side comparison reveals that the surroundings, people and movements are practically identical. The footage has been manipulated using artificial intelligence to replace Williams with Huang, repurposing a decade-old viral clip to capitalise on a major news event.

While many users shared the video humorously, comments on social media suggest that some believed the footage was genuine.

From humiliation to heroism, powered by AI

The dancing video is far from the only fabricated footage circulating in the wake of Huang's comeback.

Elon Musk, who was a vocal supporter of Huang's reinstatement, has inspired a series of AI-generated videos depicting the two tech billionaires celebrating together. Other viral memes show Huang returning from the dead or appearing as a character in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

What is particularly striking is how quickly the online narrative surrounding Nvidia's CEO has shifted.

Following his resignation, social media users flooded platforms with AI-generated videos ridiculing Huang, depicting him in embarrassing scenarios relating to his alleged affairs and departure from the company. Now, those same tools are being used to portray him as a triumphant, almost heroic figure.

While many of these videos are intended as satire rather than deliberate misinformation, there's a striking irony in the fact that one of the key architects of the AI revolution has become such a prolific subject of AI-generated content himself.

item.title: How to get your paycheck up to 2 days early: 14 banks with early direct deposit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information, but not as in-depth

When it comes to getting paid, every day counts — especially when you're facing mounting bills or even potential overdrafts. According to CNBC and SurveyMonkey's Quarterly Money Survey from July 2026, 63% of Americans said they were living paycheck to paycheck.

Some banks, credit unions and online institutions offer early direct deposit, allowing your paycheck to clear a few days before your scheduled payday. Early direct deposit is also often available for pensions, military pay and government benefits, like Social Security benefits.

In addition to giving you access to your cash sooner, setting up direct deposit can help you avoid monthly service fees and unlock other account perks.

Find out what early direct deposit is, how it works and which banks offer the service.

What is early direct deposit?

Early direct deposits provide access to paychecks and other eligible eletronic deposits one to two days before they would normally clear. If you typically get paid on a Friday, for example, you could potentially see the money in your account as early as Wednesday.

Early direct deposit is usually free and automatic if you've enroll in direct deposit. It's not a loan, though, and it's not available at every bank. Features vary depending on the financial institution and your employer's payroll process.

New direct deposits often take one to two pay cycles to start arriving early, and weekends and holidays can also shift when funds post.

How does early direct deposit work?

Employers generally submit payroll information to banks through the Automated Clearing House (ACH) network a few days before the funds actually arrive. Because they know the funds are en route, some banks will credit your account once they receive that information, rather than waiting for the traditional clearing period.

While the process is typically free and automatic, early access is not guaranteed. Check with your bank about its early deposit policy.

To set up direct deposit, you'll need to provide your bank account and routing number to your employer or fill out a direct deposit form with your bank.

Banks that offer early direct deposit

While early paycheck access is increasingly commonplace — PNC Bank just began offering it in fall 2026 — it's by no means standard. Check with your bank or credit union to see if it offers early direct deposit and if you're eligible.

Alliant Credit Union

You can qualify for Alliant Credit Union's High Rate Checking's Early Payday feature just by setting up direct deposit. The account also comes with no monthly service fees, no overdraft fees and a 0.25% APY.

Alliant is a digital-only credit union, but members have access to 80,000+ ATMs and receive up to $20 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- Earns 0.25% APY.

- 80,000 fee-free ATMs, plus up to $20 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- No overdraft fees or minimum balance requirement.

- Membership is open to anyone and Alliant will cover $5 fee.

- You must opt into paperless statements and make at least one electronic deposit per month to earn interest.

- No physical branches.

Ally Bank

The Ally Bank Spending Account offers early direct deposit automatically and your paycheck can be available up to two days early. You're limited to eight early direct deposits per account per statement cycle and each deposit must be $10,000 or less.

- 0.10% APY on balances under $15,000 and 0.25% on balances of $15,000+

- 75,000+ free ATMs and $10 per month in out-of-network ATM fee reimbursements.

- No monthly service fee, minimum opening deposit or balance requirements.

- Can get paycheck deposited up to two days early with direct deposit.

- No physical branches.

- Low APY on checking.

- Inconvenient to make cash deposits.

Axos

Early direct deposit is a free, automatic feature with both Axos Checking and the Axos ONE checking and savings bundle. Setting up direct deposit of at least $1 with Axos Checking also unlocks a 1.00% APY.

- Competitive APY for a checking account

- No monthly maintenance or overdraft fees.

- Unlimited domestic ATM fee reimbursements.

- You can receive your paycheck up to two days early through direct deposit.

- Must enroll in direct deposit to receive APY.

- No physical branches.

- Axos does not support Zelle for peer-to-peer transfers.

Capital One

The Capital One 360 Checking® account offers direct deposits up to two days early. New account holders who set up direct deposit may also qualify for one of Capital One's frequent cash welcome bonuses.

A traditional brick-and-mortar bank, Capital One has more than 250 branches and over 60 Capital One Cafés.

- Earns 0.10% APY on all balances

- No minimum opening deposit

- No overdraft fee or foreign transaction fee

- 300+ branches and Capital One cafés

- Direct deposits available up to two days early

- Over 72,000 fee-free ATMs via Capital One, Allpoint and MoneyPass networks

- Out-of-network ATM fees aren’t reimbursed

- Physical branches limited to nine states and Washington, D.C.

Chase

You can get early direct deposit automatically with Chase Secure Banking. Setting up at least $250 in qualifying monthly deposits will also get the $4.95 service fee waived.

The consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, Chase is the largest bank in the U.S., with more than 5,000 locations and 14,000 ATMs.

Chase has the largest branch network in the U.S., making its Secure Banking account a good fit if you prefer an in-person experience. We like the relatively easy-to-waive service fee and that it can function as a second-chance checking account for people rebuilding their banking history. The main drawback with Secure Banking is that it doesn't earn any interest.

- New account holders may be eligible for a cash bonus.
